name: separation-of-duties
intent: Require two or more distinct principals or components to complete a sensitive operation, so that no single account, role or object can initiate and finish it alone.
problem: A sensitive workflow is reachable end to end from one identity or one code path: the same operator creates and approves the payment, the same administrator changes the production configuration and signs it off, the same service account holds both the maker and the checker permission. The trigger is structural rather than accidental - all steps share one principal, one session, one process or one role, because splitting them costs a second pair of hands - and the failure surfaces only when an insider error or abuse is unremarkable in the audit trail: every step was authorized, because one principal held both halves of the duty.
context: Sensitive operations whose consequences must survive mistakes, coercion or misuse by authorized insiders: payments and disbursements, entitlement and permission changes, production configuration and deployment, key custody and signing, destructive data operations. It applies where identities can be kept distinct and authenticated (separate accounts, roles, services, processes), where the intermediate states of the operation can be persisted and observed, and where an enforcement point exists that can compare the acting principal with the recorded initiator - a policy engine, method security, an approval service, a separate process or account, a dual-control key ceremony. It is as much an organizational rule as a technical one: the split must follow the duties people actually hold, and recombination must be made awkward by design rather than merely discouraged.
benefits: No single credential is sufficient: a compromised account, a coerced operator or a mistaken administrator can only complete its own half, so the blast radius of one insider identity is bounded by construction.

Unilateral abuse stops being unremarkable: the audit trail records a different principal for the decisive step, so misuse needs collusion or identity theft rather than authority alone - the reduction NIST AC-5 describes as reducing malevolent activity 'without collusion'.

The duty split becomes an enumerable, reviewable artifact: which step requires which role and which pairs must never coincide can be written down, diffed and tested instead of living in habits and access reviews.
Service-side compromise is contained too: a maker service that can only create and a checker service that can only release cannot be tricked into completing each other's job.

It makes the other security rules pay off: least privilege defines the halves, complete mediation enforces them, fail-safe defaults deny the missing approval, and audit records two actors where one would otherwise be enough.
tradeoffs: Throughput and availability: a sensitive operation now waits for a second principal, so the workflow acquires a queue, timeouts and an escalation path, and an absent approver blocks the action rather than merely slowing it.

It does not stop collusion or an attacker who holds both identities: separation of duties raises the cost of unilateral action; it is a layer, not a proof, and NIST's wording ('without collusion') is the honest scope.

Identity bookkeeping becomes a correctness problem: shared named accounts, one person holding two roles, a service account with both permissions or an administrator who can grant the missing half silently recombine what the design separated.

Friction breeds workarounds: during incidents, migrations and holidays the second approval is inconvenient, so break-glass paths and standing exceptions appear - and unless they are named, time-bounded and audited, they become the real production posture and discredit the rule.

State complexity moves into the application: partially approved work needs persisted intermediate states, expiry and withdrawal semantics, and approvals bound to the reviewed version of the request, or an edited request rides on a stale approval.

It adds a second place to get authorization wrong: a predicate that lives in the UI, trusts client-supplied identity or is checked outside the enforcement point can be bypassed by calling the endpoint directly.

participants.responsibility: The authenticated principal that performs the first, sensitive step - create the payment, request the entitlement, prepare the migration, propose the configuration change. Its authority stops short of the terminal outcome; it must not hold the approval right.

A distinct authenticated principal that performs the decisive second step. Its approval is insufficient without the initiator's work, and its value lies exactly in coming from a different identity with its own credentials and accountability.

The persisted object whose state machine records who initiated and who approved, refuses the terminal transition until the required distinct steps have happened, and binds each approval to the version that was reviewed.

The reviewed mapping from duties to roles and principals, including the pairs that must never coincide (maker/checker, developer/production release, access-control administration/audit administration); it is what access authorizations are derived from.

Where the distinct-principal predicate is actually evaluated and the step is refused - a policy engine or method-security interceptor, the service method performing the transition, a separate process or OS account boundary, a dual-control key ceremony. A check that the code can bypass is not this role.

use_cases: Maker-checker payments: an operator above a threshold creates a disbursement and a second operator releases it; the ledger records both identities and refuses a release signed by the maker.

Change control and deployment: production IAM policy or infrastructure changes require a second administrator's approval, and the pipeline refuses to run a change approved by its own author (required reviewers / second signature).

Key custody and dual control: signing keys or root credentials are split so two authorized operators must each contribute a share (split knowledge, m-of-n threshold, dual-control key ceremony) and no single share can sign.

Access provisioning: the requester of an entitlement, its approver and the administrator who grants it are three distinct roles; the administrator cannot approve their own request, and access-control administrators do not administer the audit log.
Destructive data operations: schema migrations, production data edits and deletion jobs are prepared by one engineer and executed by a different operator account that cannot author the change.
Regulated back-office workflows: journal entries, refunds, credit adjustments and account closures are initiated by one clerk and posted by another, with the pairing recorded for audit.

GitHub protected branches: a pull request targeting a protected branch needs the configured number of approving reviews before it can merge, the platform refuses an approval from the PR author by design, and with dismiss-stale-review enabled a commit pushed after the review voids the approval - four-eyes enforced at the merge gate with the approval bound to the reviewed revision.

AWS Systems Manager Change Manager: a change request may run its Automation runbook only after approvals from named IAM users, groups or roles arrive across up to five approval levels, and a single rejection stops execution; because change templates list approvers separately from requesters, a request submitted under one IAM principal is released by another.

HashiCorp Vault key custody: vault operator init splits the root key with Shamir's Secret Sharing into key shares (default 5) under a threshold (default 3); unsealing or generating a root token needs a quorum of distinct share holders, and PGP-encrypting each share for a named operator makes dual control a property of the mechanism rather than of the procedure.
avoid_when: Single-operator, low-blast-radius or reversible actions where a second approval adds latency without changing risk: a typed confirmation, a dry run or an undo/audit trail is the simpler answer.

The platform already provides the control structurally (four-eyes change approval in the deployment pipeline, dual-signature release in the signing service, threshold key custody in the KMS): configure it instead of building a second approval silo on top.

Real-time operations where a human second party cannot be in the loop (autonomous control, latency-critical trading): prefer automatic controls, rate limits and after-the-fact audit, or make the operation reversible - do not invent a fake approver.

Genuinely emergency or break-glass actions (incident response, disaster recovery): an audited, time-bounded single-actor path with post-hoc review is more honest than a split that will be bypassed under pressure.

Teams so small that the two roles unavoidably land on the same person: the rule becomes theater; compensate with logging, stronger authentication and platform boundaries, and do not claim a separation that does not exist.
anti_patterns: Shared accounts or one person holding both roles: the workflow has two steps but one actor, and a check for 'different username' passes while the real separation does not exist.

The self-approval path: the endpoint that approves a request never compares the approver's identity with the initiator's (or hides the button in the UI but allows the call), so the same principal completes both steps.
Four-eyes as documentation: the design requires two approvers while the deployment ships one administrator role with both permissions, or an admin who can grant themselves the missing half.

Approval of an editable object: the approver reviews version N while the maker can still change the request after approval, so the released operation was never the one that was approved (a TOCTOU between approval and execution).
Exception creep: standing break-glass access or 'temporary' combinations of duties that are never revoked, so the split exists only in the policy document.
The fake second party: an automated bot or the same human under a second account counts as the approver, turning the two-step into a ceremony that satisfies the letter of the rule.
design_principles: Separation of privilege and of duties (Saltzer & Schroeder, 1975, principle e): a mechanism that requires two keys is more robust and lets the keys be physically separated, with distinct programs, organizations or individuals made responsible for them, so no single accident, deception or breach of trust is sufficient to compromise the protected operation.
Least privilege per step: each duty carries only the rights its own step needs, or the split is undone by a role that could perform every step anyway.
Complete mediation and fail-safe defaults: the distinct-principal check must sit at the enforcement point on every access path, and a missing approval must deny rather than default to allowed.

Least common mechanism and single responsibility: do not let the machinery that holds one half of the authority also hold the other (one session, one credential, one role able to do both), and keep each duty owned by exactly one accountable party.
Defence in depth: separation of duties limits unilateral insider action and complements authentication strength, monitoring and audit; it is a layer, not a proof of security.
best_practices: Model and persist the intermediate states (initiated_by, reviewed revision, approved_by), and make the terminal transition impossible without a distinct second principal's authenticated action at the enforcement point - not merely hidden in the UI.

Enforce at the enforcement point on every path (API, service method, policy engine, process boundary) and compare stable principal identifiers from the authenticated context, never client-supplied identity fields or display names.

Keep the duty split as a reviewed artifact: list the duties, the roles that may hold them and the pairs that must never coincide, and re-review it when the organization or the deployment topology changes (NIST AC-5: identify and document the duties; define system access authorizations to support separation of duties).
Bind each approval to the reviewed version of the request and void or expire it when the request changes; make re-approval cheap and explicit instead of silently carrying an old approval forward.

Make recombination operationally hard, not merely impermissible: separate accounts, separate teams, separate credentials; let access-control administration and audit administration stay with different people, and keep production execution separate from production authoring.
Keep a named break-glass path that is time-bounded, logged and reviewed after use, so the honest exception does not grow into a permanent bypass of the split.
sources: Schumacher, Fernandez-Buglioni, Hybertson, Buschmann & Sommerlad, Security Patterns: Integrating Security and Systems Engineering, Wiley 2006 - security design principles including separation of duties, part of the security-patterns canon referenced by this catalog's Section 8.

Nagappan & Steel, Core Security Patterns: Best Practices and Strategies for J2EE, Web Services, and Identity Management (2005) - the second reference this catalog lists for its security patterns in Section 8; its treatment of authorization and accountability includes the split of duties across roles.

Saltzer & Schroeder, The Protection of Information in Computer Systems, Proceedings of the IEEE 63(9), 1975 - design principle (e) separation of privilege: a mechanism that requires two keys is more robust; once locked, the keys can be physically separated and distinct programs, organizations or individuals made responsible for them, so no single accident, deception or breach of trust is sufficient.

NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, AC-5 Separation of Duties: identify and document the duties of individuals and define system access authorizations to support separation of duties; combines dividing functions among different individuals or roles, conducting support functions with different individuals, and ensuring that access-control administrators do not also administer audit.

OWASP Developer Guide, Principles of security (Separation of Duties): the successful completion of a single task depends on two or more conditions that are insufficient, individually by themselves, for completing the task - limiting the damage an aggrieved or malicious insider can do and restricting privilege escalation.

OWASP Secure Product Design Cheat Sheet: separation of duties as a fundamental principle of internal control - no single individual has control over all aspects of a transaction; different tasks are assigned to different people.

GitHub Docs, About protected branches: protected branches can require a set number of approving reviews (optionally from code owners) before a pull request merges and can dismiss stale approvals when new commits are pushed; the PR author's own approval never counts, so merging requires a second principal.

AWS Systems Manager Change Manager user guide, About approvals in your change templates: change requests must be approved by designated approvers - IAM users, groups or roles across up to five approval levels - before the Automation runbook executes, and one rejection prevents execution.

HashiCorp Vault documentation, Seal/Unseal and operator init: the root key is split via Shamir's Secret Sharing into unseal key shares with a configurable threshold (defaults: 5 shares, quorum 3); unsealing and root-token generation require that quorum of distinct holders, so no single key holder can unseal.

Sasse & Bartsch, How Users Bypass Access Control - And Why (2013): authorization friction drives real users to circumvent controls - workarounds, multiple accounts and password sharing among co-workers - so a duty split that ignores operational pressure is dissolved in practice by shared credentials and temporary privilege creep; the fix is a named, expedited exception path, not a stricter prohibition.
